{gratia} 0.12.1 gives sampling arguments the same meaning across
`posterior_samples()`, `fitted_samples()`, `smooth_samples()`,
`derivative_samples()`, their `add_*()` helpers, and coefficient draw functions.
Name the sampling arguments in your calls. You can still pass the model by
position, or both data and model in `add_*()` helpers. If you use an obsolete
argument, the error message names its replacement where available.

## Replace the draw-count and grid arguments

`n_draws` is the total number of draws to retain across all chains. For
example, `n_draws = 1000` with `chains = 4` retains 250 draws per chain. Supply
`n_draws` explicitly when generating samples and choose a multiple of the
number of chains. `chains = NULL` uses one chain or reads the chain identities
from supplied coefficient draws.

| Previous argument | Replacement |
|:------------------|:------------|
| `n` in fitted, posterior, predicted, smooth and coefficient sampling | `n_draws` |
| `n_sim` in derivative sampling | `n_draws` |
| `n` in derivative sampling | `n_grid` |
| `n_vals` in smooth sampling | `n_grid` |
| `object` in derivative sampling | `model` |
| `object` in `add_*()` sampling helpers | `data` |
| `freq` | `frequentist` |
| `newdata` | `data` |
| `ncores` | `n_cores` for MH chains; `n_threads` for Gaussian draws |
| `n_cores` for Gaussian sampling | `n_threads` |
| `term` in smooth sampling | `select` |

For example, the previous derivative call

```r
# Previous interface; now produces an informative error.
derivative_samples(model, focal = "x", n = 100, n_sim = 1000)
```

becomes

```r
# 1,000 retained coefficient draws, evaluated at 100 points.
derivative_samples(model, focal = "x", n_draws = 1000, n_grid = 100)
```

`n_grid = 200` is the common default for smooth and derivative sampling.
For smooths, it supplies the resolution to `smooth_data()`; multidimensional
smooths can contain more rows than `n_grid`. Derivative sampling constructs a
slice along `focal`, holding other variables at representative values. Explicit
`data` determine the evaluation locations instead of `n_grid`. Use explicit
`data` when the exact grid matters. Fitted and response sampling use fitting
observations when `data = NULL` and do not construct a grid.

## Run several sampling chains

The example below runs four Metropolis–Hastings (MH) chains, each starting
its own sampling sequence. It retains 1,000 draws in total and requests
diagnostics to check how well the chains explore the coefficient distribution.
These examples use placeholder model objects; substitute your own fitted
models when updating an analysis.

```r
samples <- fitted_samples(
  model, n_draws = 1000, chains = 4, n_cores = 4,
  method = "mh", burnin = 1000, thin = 1,
  diagnostics = TRUE, seed = 281
)
diagnostics <- sampling_diagnostics(samples)
diagnostics
# These plots describe the coefficient chains used for the fitted samples.
draw(diagnostics, select = 1:2)
draw(diagnostics, type = "rank", select = 1:2)
```

Each chain discards its first 1,000 iterations (the burn-in), whether run in
parallel or in sequence. `thin = 2` retains every
second iteration after burn-in and still returns `n_draws` draws in total.
`n_cores` limits concurrent MH chains using {mirai}, capped at `chains`. An
existing worker pool is reused; otherwise temporary workers are cleaned up
automatically. Given the same seed and sampler backend, retained draws agree
between serial and parallel runs.

Gaussian sampling uses `n_threads` to control threads inside {mvnfast}. It does
not run concurrent MH chains. A control explicitly supplied to a method that
cannot use it produces an error, including MH controls for Gaussian draws or
Gaussian covariance controls for MH. `block_size` and `dense_limit` apply only
to `method = "mh", mh_backend = "gratia"`.

`mh_backend` chooses the implementation used to evaluate the model likelihood
and run MH sampling. The default is `"mgcv"`; the alternatives extend the
supported models or reduce memory use:

| `mh_backend` | Evaluation | Model support |
|:-------------|:-----------|:--------------|
| `"mgcv"` | `mgcv::gam.mh()` | Its existing `gam` support |
| `"gratia"` | Compiled likelihoods and MH loop | Gaussian identity, Poisson log, binomial logit, Gamma log, and negative binomial log `gam` and independent-observation `bam` fits |
| `"family"` | Compiled MH loop with callbacks to the fitted family | Compatible standard, extended, and general {mgcv} families, including independent-observation `bam` fits |

For example, a multinomial fit can use the family evaluator without a separate
compiled multinomial likelihood:

```r
samples <- posterior_samples(
  model, n_draws = 1000, chains = 4, n_cores = 4,
  method = "mh", mh_backend = "family",
  burnin = 1000, diagnostics = TRUE, seed = 281
)
```

The `"family"` implementation uses the fitted family's likelihood functions
and retains the full model matrix in memory, including for models fitted by
`bam()`. For a supported family with a model matrix too large to retain,
choose `"gratia"` to evaluate subsets of rows in turn. Both implementations
evaluate discrete `bam()` models at the original covariate values.

The `"gratia"` and `"family"` backends require a model likelihood for
independent observations and reject fits with AR1 dependence or GAMM
components. They also reject fits using `paraPen`, `H` or a pre-fit `G`
object, or with a singular coefficient covariance matrix.
The family backend additionally rejects quasi families, which do not provide
a likelihood, and Cox proportional hazards models. All three MH backends
condition on fitted smoothing, dispersion, and any family parameters outside
the coefficient vector. Parameters represented by coefficients are sampled,
including scale or covariance coefficients in general families.
`unconditional = TRUE` applies to Gaussian sampling only.

## Reuse the same coefficient draws for several quantities

Generate coefficients once when you want smooth contributions or predictions
to share the same draws. Here `method = "user"` passes an existing coefficient
matrix to `smooth_samples()` and `fitted_samples()`:

```r
betas <- post_draws(model, n_draws = 1000, chains = 4, seed = 281)
fitted <- fitted_samples(model, method = "user", draws = betas)
smooth <- smooth_samples(model, method = "user", draws = betas)
derivative <- derivative_samples(
  model, focal = "x", method = "user", draws = betas
)
```

The coefficient matrix determines the count and chain layout. Explicit
`n_draws` or `chains` must agree with it. A plain matrix without chain metadata
represents one chain; chain boundaries are never guessed from the row count.
Smooths always transform the same joint coefficient draws. The old
`rng_per_smooth` option is removed because independently redrawing each smooth
loses their posterior dependence. The previously ignored `mu`, `sigma`, and
derivative `level` arguments are also rejected.

Multiple-chain tables retain `.chain`, `.iteration`, and globally unique `.draw`
columns. Single-chain tables keep their previous columns. Attached diagnostics
refer to coefficients before transformation or response simulation.
`as_mcmc_draws()` converts coefficient matrices or sampled quantities for
{posterior} or {coda} diagnostics. Optional packages are required only when their
formats or diagnostics are requested.

`draw(sampling_diagnostics(x))` displays the retained coefficient draws in
iteration order for each chain. With thinning, successive points can be
several sampler iterations apart. Use `type = "rank"` with at least two
chains to see whether each chain covers the full range of pooled ranks.
Tied values receive their average rank. Each chain gets a histogram, with a
reference line for equal counts across bins. Use `select` to choose coefficients
by name or position. If `x` contains sampled fitted values, responses, smooths
or derivatives, set `diagnostics = TRUE` when generating them to retain their
coefficient draws. The plots are provided by gratia. Numerical summaries
require posterior.

## Choose between expected values and simulated observations

`fitted_samples()` draws distribution parameters by default; use
`quantity = "expectation"` for expected responses. `smooth_samples()` draws
individual smooth contributions, and `derivative_samples()` draws derivatives.
`posterior_samples()` also simulates response variation for each coefficient
draw. `predicted_samples()` simulates responses with fitted parameters held
fixed. It uses `n_draws` for the number of response replicates and rejects
coefficient-chain controls; use `posterior_samples()` to include coefficient
uncertainty.

Model-specific capabilities still apply. For example, the native diagnostic
samplers for `lm` and mixed models support Gaussian approximations and fitting
observations only, and reject unsupported chain controls. See
`help("diagnostic_support")` for model-specific support. Functions that summarise
draws, such as `response_derivatives()` and `conditional_differences()`, keep
their existing grid and simulation-count arguments; their internal sampling
calls use this interface.

## Update likelihood, model comparison and predictive check calls

`log_lik()`, `loo::loo()`, `loo::waic()` and `bayesplot::pp_check()` use the
same `n_draws` convention. Likelihood, leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) and
WAIC calls default to 4,000 draws. For {bayesplot}, gratia uses 50 for ordinary
checks and 4,000 for leave-one-out plots.
Supplied coefficient matrices determine their own counts. Pass `chains`,
`diagnostics`, `method` and backend controls directly to `log_lik()`, or through
`sampling_args` for LOO, WAIC and bayesplot. Likelihood matrices and these
diagnostic results retain the coefficient sampling metadata. LOO reads stored
chain iterations when estimating how much autocorrelation affects the effective
sample size, while keeping likelihood and response draws in their original
order. Unlabelled supplied matrices
still require explicit `chain_id` or `r_eff` for LOO. The old `n` argument and
explicit controls for a different sampler produce errors.

## Sample models with several distribution parameters

Location-scale-shape (LSS) models can use separate predictors for distribution
parameters such as the mean and standard deviation. `posterior_samples()`
now accepts evaluation data for `gaulss()`, `gammals()`,
`gumbls()`, `gevlss()`, `shash()`, `twlss()` and `ziplss()` fits. Supply covariates
and formula-offset variables; observed responses are unnecessary. Every
predictor uses the same joint coefficient draw. For example:

```r
# Evaluate the first 200 observations, retaining their joint parameter draws.
b <- post_draws(model, n_draws = 1000, chains = 4, seed = 281)
y <- posterior_samples(model, data = evaluation_data[1:200, ],
  method = "user", draws = b, seed = 282)
```

The functions return different quantities:

| Function | Quantity for an LSS model |
|:---------|:--------------------------|
| `fitted_samples(scale = "response")` | Distribution parameters in their usual units, such as mean and standard deviation |
| `fitted_samples(scale = "linear_predictor")` | All parameter predictors, in family order |
| `fitted_samples(quantity = "expectation")` | Expected response, using every parameter on which it depends |
| `posterior_samples()` | Responses conditional on each joint coefficient draw |
| `predicted_samples()` | Responses conditional on the fixed fitted coefficients |
| `derivative_samples(scale = "response")` | Derivative of the expected response, retaining joint coefficient uncertainty |
| `derivative_samples(scale = "linear_predictor")` | Derivative of the first predictor |
| `smooth_samples()` | Selected smooth contribution to its own predictor |

The `.parameter` column labels each parameter by its meaning on both scales.
Expectation output uses `.parameter = "expectation"`. Gumbel, GEV and
sinh-arcsinh means generally differ from location; the hurdle Poisson mean
uses both predictors and accounts for zero truncation. A GEV mean does not
exist at shape >= 1; requesting that mean or its derivative gives an error,
while parameter and response draws remain available.

`gaulss()` represents its second response parameter as inverse SD. Sampling
uses its reciprocal and divides SD by the square root of an explicit sampling
weight. The native `gaulss()` likelihood ignores fitting weights; default response
weights are ones, preserving the fitted likelihood and existing diagnostic rules.
The other LSS response generators currently ignore sampling weights, as their
mgcv implementations do. Formula offsets are evaluated at supplied covariates;
stored fitting offsets are retained with `data = NULL`. The installed mgcv
version rejects offsets when fitting `shash()` and drops call-level offsets
for general-family fits; gratia cannot reconstruct offsets never applied by
the fitter. Prefer supported formula offsets.

## Identify the response family for each prediction row

`posterior_samples()` also accepts fitting-data subsets and new covariates for
`mgcv::gfam()` models. Every row must identify its component family, either
through the response-index expression in the supplied data or through
`family_index`. Observed response values are not needed. For example:

```r
posterior_samples(grouped_model, data = evaluation_data,
  family_index = component_index, n_draws = 1000, chains = 4, seed = 281)
```

The same joint coefficient draw is used for every component. Each component
uses its own link and any other fitted family parameters, such as dispersion.
Offsets in the model formula are evaluated at the supplied covariates. New-data
sampling weights default to one; explicit weights override them. Output retains
`.parameter = "component1"`, `"component2"`, and so on, together with `.row`,
`.draw` and any chain columns. Missing predictors, membership or sampling weights
produce missing responses. Fitting rows excluded by `na.exclude()` are restored.
Smooth samples retain their predictor contributions, and response derivatives
use each row's component mean. For derivatives, membership must be recoverable
from `data`; `derivative_samples()` does not accept `family_index`.
Ordinal expectations and their derivatives refer to category probabilities,
identified by `.category`. Scalar components have `NA` in that column.
Censored grouped components require an observation process
for posterior response sampling; use `simulate()` for latent uncensored draws.

MH coefficient sampling rejects BAM fits with nonzero prescribed smooth
contributions, such as a nonzero soap-film boundary. Native fitting and
prediction can use different offsets for those fits. Supplied coefficient
draws can still be evaluated with the native prediction conventions.

## Interpret draws for censored and survival responses

Censored-family generators draw the underlying response before censoring.
To compare simulated and observed responses in a posterior predictive check,
apply the same censoring process to the simulated data. Response sampling
through this interface is unavailable for Cox proportional hazards models.

## Distribution parameters and expected responses

`fitted_values()` and `fitted_samples()` now default to
`quantity = "parameters"`. They return each parameter represented by a
predictor, including an intercept-only predictor, in its usual units.
Use `family_parameters(model)` to inspect the names, definitions, predictor
order and native representation. Global parameters appear in that description
but remain fixed during coefficient sampling.

Use `quantity = "expectation"` to request the expected response. Expectations
are available only on the response scale. Use `scale = "link"` with parameter
output for the model predictors. A Gaussian location-scale model returns
`mean` and `sd`. A GEV model returns `location`, `scale` and `shape`, and its
location generally differs from its expectation. The hurdle Poisson model
fitted with `ziplss()` returns `rate` and `presence_probability`. Its
expectation accounts for the fact that the count distribution describes
positive counts only.

The following calls contrast parameter output with expected responses. For a
Gaussian location-scale model, the latter returns only the mean. For a
`ziplss()` model, the mean depends on both predictors.

```r
family_parameters(model)
fitted_samples(model, n_draws = 100, quantity = "parameters")
fitted_samples(model, n_draws = 100, quantity = "expectation")
fitted_values(model, quantity = "expectation")
```

For categorical models, expectation output contains category probabilities.
Categories and multivariate responses use `.category` and `.y`, separately
from `.parameter`. Expected responses use `.parameter = "expectation"`.
`posterior_samples()` draws new observations after drawing coefficients;
`predicted_samples()` draws observations with fitted coefficients held fixed.
Neither is a substitute for draws of an expectation.

### Location, rate and expectation

For these calls, assume you have fitted `gev_fit` with `mgcv::gevlss()`,
`zip_fit` with `mgcv::ziplss()`, and `tw_fit` with `mgcv::twlss()` to appropriate
response data. The calls show which output to request from each model: its
distribution parameters or its expected response. The
[response-distributions article](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/response-distributions.html) explains how
distributional predictors affect predictions and model checks.

```r
family_parameters(gev_fit)
fitted_values(gev_fit) # location, scale and shape
fitted_values(gev_fit, quantity = "expectation")

fitted_samples(zip_fit, n_draws = 5) # rate and presence probability
fitted_samples(zip_fit, n_draws = 5, quantity = "expectation")

fitted_values(tw_fit) # mean, power and dispersion
fitted_values(tw_fit, quantity = "expectation") # equals the mean parameter
```

For `ziplss()`, writing rate as lambda and presence probability as p,
the expectation is `p * lambda / (1 - exp(-lambda))`. The denominator
accounts for the zero-truncated Poisson distribution of positive counts.
GEV location generally differs from its expectation. Tweedie's mean parameter
is already its expectation, but its power and dispersion are separate parameters.
